newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Clinton learns from golf game with Norman.
newsitem.headline: Clinton learns from golf game with Norman.

text.p: Living a duffer's dream, U.S. President Bill Clinton took to the fairways on Thursday with Australian golfing legend Greg Norman -- and soon found himself getting lessons from the game's ultimate teacher.
Teeing off at the New South Wales Golf Club, Clinton was asked how he felt playing with the world's top player. "Terrified," he said with a smile.
When asked what his primary goal was, Clinton replied: "Stay out of trouble." Clinton patiently stood over his ball and swung hard, hooking the ball. "Too far left," he muttered.

Norman, standing behind the president, asked: "Are you going to take another?" Clinton, an avid amateur with a fondness for "mulligans" -- which let a player try again without it appearing in his score -- replied: "Are you going to count it?"

Both men laughed, and the ground rules were clear. Clinton set up another ball and hit it down the fairway. Norman, known as "The Shark" because of his extraordinary competitiveness and his love for deep sea fishing, needed only one swing to put his ball where he wanted it.
The two also played with John Coates, president of Australia's Olympic Committee, and Ted Kunkel, chief executive officer of the Fosters beer company.

The 72-par, 6,227-meter course, nestled on the edge of historic Botany Bay -- where Captain James Cook landed in 1770 -- is considered one of Australia's toughest because of the stiff winds the sweep the course.

The president, known as "the world's most powerful man," and Norman, the world's number one golfer, quickly set aside the competitiveness in the worlds they live in. Clinton became the willing student and Norman the willing teacher.
A small pool of journalists was allowed to witness only two other holes played -- the fifth and sixth, and on both Norman was clearly passing on his knowledge.
Clinton was paying strict attention, and still relying on mulligans -- a rule he again invoked on the fifth hole, but probably wished he hadn't.

Clinton's first drive went awry so he tried it again, sending his second one into a sand trap. After Norman climbed down into the steep trap to continue his lessons, Clinton needed only one swing to get his ball back on the fairway.

On the sixth hole, each player was required to tee up and drive their golf ball over a rocky cliff, have it sail over the swirling waters of the bay and have it land on the fairway. If it didn't reach the fairway, it was destined for the ultimate water hazard below.

Norman could be seen having a detailed discussion with Clinton, pointing as he spoke. The presidential duffer swung away and sent the ball safely to the green. Norman did the same thing, only his ball landed much closer to the pin.
As they were getting ready to head off for the seventh tee, Norman was asked how the game was going. Australia's newest diplomat flashed his smile and said, "He's beating me."
Clinton kept walking away, but then turned around with a wide grin. "If you believe that, I've got a little land I want to show you," he joked.
Then the student and the teacher got into their golf cart and drove off, with the grateful pupil driving.
